title: Dissection of Cubes
description: Wiedijk 100 theorem #82: a cube cannot be dissected into a finite number of smaller cubes all of different sizes. Proved by Littlewood (1953) via infinite descent — the smallest cube on any horizontal floor is surrounded by taller cubes, so its top face becomes a new floor with smaller cubes, generating an infinitely long strictly decreasing chain that contradicts finiteness. Contrasts with 2D, where perfect squared squares DO exist (Brooks-Smith-Stone-Tutte, 1940). Formalized in 366 lines with 2 axioms capturing the 3D geometric covering argument.

overview.historicalContext:
The question of whether a cube can be dissected into smaller cubes of all different sizes emerged from the broader study of geometric dissection problems. Max Dehn's 1903 paper 'Über die Zerlegung von Rechtecken in Rechtecke' initiated the systematic study of rectangle and square dissections. The analogous 2D question — can a square be dissected into squares of all different sizes? — was posed as a puzzle by Zbigniew Moron in 1925 and became known as 'squaring the square.'

The 2D problem was solved affirmatively in a remarkable 1940 paper by four Cambridge undergraduates: R.L. Brooks, C.A.B. Smith, A.H. Stone, and W.T. Tutte. They discovered an extraordinary connection between squared rectangles and electrical networks: interpreting horizontal cuts as nodes and vertical square boundaries as resistors, they showed that every squared rectangle corresponds to a planar resistor network (the 'Smith diagram'). Using Kirchhoff's laws to analyze these networks, they found perfect squared rectangles and eventually squared squares. Tutte later recalled that the problem arose from a puzzle in H.E. Dudeney's 'Canterbury Puzzles' (1907).

The first perfect squared squares found were compound (containing smaller squared sub-rectangles). The simplest 'simple perfect squared square' — one with no squared sub-rectangle — was found by A.J.W. Duijvestijn in 1978, after an exhaustive computer search: it has 21 squares with side lengths from 2 to 50, arranged in a 112×112 frame.

The 3D impossibility was proved by J.E. Littlewood and included in his delightful book 'A Mathematician's Miscellany' (1953). The proof is a model of mathematical elegance — it requires no computation, no algebra, just geometric visualization and the method of infinite descent. The key geometric insight: in a 3D cube dissection with all different sizes, the smallest cube resting on any horizontal face is completely surrounded by taller cubes on all four vertical sides (since all sizes are different). This forces the top face of the smallest cube to be a new interior 'floor,' entirely contained within the original cube, covered by cubes that must be even smaller. Repeating this argument yields an infinite strictly decreasing sequence of cube sizes — contradicting the assumption that only finitely many cubes were used.

The contrast between 2D and 3D is striking: in 2D, a small square on the bottom edge can extend to the side wall of the enclosing square, escaping the 'surrounding' argument. In 3D, no cube on the bottom face can reach all four side walls simultaneously (since it would then be a full layer, not a smaller cube). The impossibility extends to all dimensions $n \geq 3$ and to dissections of rectangular boxes into cubes of all different sizes.
overview.problemStatement:
**Theorem (Littlewood)**: A cube cannot be dissected into a finite number of smaller cubes, all of different sizes.

Equivalently: In any dissection of a cube into finitely many smaller cubes, at least two cubes must have the same size.

This is Wiedijk's 100 Theorems #82.
overview.text:
This formalization proves that a cube cannot be dissected into finitely many smaller cubes all of different sizes — a result known as the impossibility of perfect cubed cube dissection. The proof uses Littlewood's infinite descent argument: consider the bottom face of the large cube, which must be tiled by the bottom faces of smaller cubes. The smallest such face is not against any wall (it would be surrounded by larger squares), so the cube above it creates a new smaller tiling problem on its top face, leading to an infinite descent.

The file establishes the contrast with 2D (perfect squared squares DO exist — the smallest has side 112 with 21 squares) and the connection to electrical network theory (squared rectangles correspond to planar resistor networks via the Smith diagram). Commentary discusses the generalization to higher dimensions and Brooks-Smith-Stone-Tutte's work connecting dissection problems to graph theory.
overview.proofStrategy:
**Littlewood's Proof by Infinite Descent**:

1. Consider the bottom face of the large cube, covered by smaller cubes
2. Find the smallest cube touching the bottom — call it C (via `Finset.exists_min_image`)
3. Since all sizes differ, C is surrounded by taller cubes on all sides
4. C's top face becomes a new 'floor' at a higher level
5. This floor is covered by cubes smaller than C
6. Repeat: generates an infinite strictly decreasing sequence of cube sizes
7. A strictly decreasing chain of length n requires n distinct cubes (injectivity via `Fintype.card_le_of_injective`)
8. Take a chain of length card+1 > card — contradiction with finiteness (`omega`)
keyInsights: **Pure Geometry, No Computation**: Littlewood's proof requires no algebra, no analysis, no number theory — just geometric visualization and the method of infinite descent. This makes it one of the most elegant impossibility proofs in mathematics, alongside the irrationality of $\sqrt{2}$ and the non-denumerability of $\mathbb{R}$

**The 2D/3D Dichotomy**: In 2D, perfect squared squares exist (smallest: 21 squares, side 112). In 3D, they're impossible. The geometric reason: in 3D, a small cube on the floor is surrounded on all 4 vertical sides by taller cubes (since all sizes differ). In 2D, a corner square touches two walls simultaneously, blocking the descent. This dimensional phase transition at $n = 3$ has no analogue in most other geometric problems

**Axiomatization Strategy**: The two axioms (`smaller_cube_above_axiom`, `all_different_implies_long_chains_axiom`) encapsulate the 3D geometric covering argument — the claim that the smallest cube on any floor is surrounded and produces a smaller floor above. Formalizing this requires 3D tiling theory and interval arithmetic beyond current Lean/Mathlib capabilities. The axiomatization is honest: these are the non-trivial geometric facts, while the combinatorial consequence (chain → contradiction) is fully proved

**Chain Length Bounded (Proved)**: The key proved lemma `chain_length_bounded` shows that a strictly decreasing chain of cube sizes is injective (distinct cubes have distinct sizes), so its length is bounded by $|\text{cubes}|$ via `Fintype.card_le_of_injective`. This reduces the infinite descent argument to a finite pigeonhole: take a chain of length $|\text{cubes}| + 1$ and derive $|\text{cubes}| + 1 \leq |\text{cubes}|$, closed by `omega`

**Electrical Network Connection**: Brooks-Smith-Stone-Tutte's solution to 2D squaring uses a remarkable bijection between squared rectangles and planar resistor networks. Horizontal cuts become nodes, squares become resistors with resistance = side length, and Kirchhoff's current law enforces the geometric constraints. This Smith diagram technique has no known 3D analogue — part of why the 3D question has a different answer

**The Infinite Descent Pattern**: The proof pattern (assume P → construct arbitrarily long decreasing chain → chain is injective → length bounded by $|S|$ → contradiction) appears across combinatorics: in the Erdős-Szekeres theorem (monotone subsequences), Ramsey theory (monochromatic cliques), and Dilworth's theorem (antichains in posets). The formalization makes this pattern explicit via `hasDecreasingChain` and `chain_length_bounded`

**Dimensional Generalization**: The impossibility extends to all dimensions $n \geq 3$: in $\mathbb{R}^n$, the smallest $n$-cube on any $(n-1)$-dimensional 'floor' is surrounded on all $2(n-1)$ vertical sides by taller cubes, producing the same descent. The threshold is sharp: $n = 2$ allows perfect dissections, $n \geq 3$ does not

conclusion.summary: Littlewood's proof elegantly shows that cube dissection into different-sized cubes is impossible through infinite descent. The smallest cube resting on any horizontal 'floor' is surrounded by taller cubes on all four vertical sides, so its top face becomes a new interior floor covered by even smaller cubes. Repeating this generates an infinitely long strictly decreasing chain of cube sizes — contradicting the finiteness of the dissection. The Lean formalization captures this in 366 lines: two axioms encode the 3D geometric covering argument, while `chain_length_bounded` (proved via `Fintype.card_le_of_injective`) and the main theorem (3 lines + `omega`) handle the combinatorial contradiction.
conclusion.implications:
**1. 2D/3D Contrast**: The 2D analog (squaring the square) IS possible — Brooks-Smith-Stone-Tutte (1940) found the first examples, and Duijvestijn (1978) found the smallest simple perfect squared square (21 squares, side 112). The dimensional phase transition at $n = 3$ is remarkable: a purely geometric property of space changes qualitatively between 2 and 3 dimensions.

**2. Electrical Network Theory**: The 2D solution exploits a deep connection between squared rectangles and planar resistor networks (Smith diagram). Kirchhoff's laws enforce the geometric constraints of square tiling. No analogous network interpretation exists for 3D cube dissection, which may explain the impossibility.

**3. Infinite Descent as a Proof Pattern**: The proof pattern — construct a strictly decreasing chain, bound its length by pigeonhole, derive a contradiction — is a recurring technique in combinatorics. It appears in the Erdős-Szekeres theorem (monotone subsequences), Ramsey theory (monochromatic cliques), Dilworth's theorem (antichains in posets), and the proof that every Noetherian ring has the ascending chain condition.

**4. Formalization Gap**: The two axioms represent a genuine formalization gap: proving that the smallest cube on a floor is surrounded requires formal 3D geometry (interval analysis, tiling theory) beyond current Lean/Mathlib capabilities. This is a concrete target for future formalization work.

**5. Dimensional Generalization**: The impossibility extends to all dimensions $n \geq 3$ and to rectangular boxes dissected into cubes. In $\mathbb{R}^n$ ($n \geq 3$), the smallest $n$-cube on any hyperplane floor is surrounded on all $2(n-1)$ vertical faces, producing the same descent.
openQuestions: What is the minimum number of size-repeated cubes required in any cube dissection? The theorem shows at least 2 cubes must share sizes, but the tight bound is unknown.
Can a tetrahedron be dissected into tetrahedra of all different sizes? The surrounding argument relies on axis-alignment; non-axis-aligned shapes may behave differently.

Can the geometric covering axioms (`smaller_cube_above_axiom`, `all_different_implies_long_chains_axiom`) be proved without external axioms? This requires formalizing 3D interval geometry: that the smallest axis-aligned cube on a face is surrounded by taller cubes on all 4 sides.

Is there a connection between cube dissection impossibility and the Dehn invariant? Dehn's theorem (Hilbert's 3rd problem) shows that equidecomposability of polyhedra requires matching Dehn invariants — could a similar invariant obstruct cube dissection?
Can the electrical network connection for 2D squaring be generalized to higher dimensions? A 3D 'Smith diagram' analogue might explain why 3D dissection fails from a network-theoretic perspective.

What is the computational complexity of determining whether a given collection of cube sizes can tile a larger cube (allowing repeated sizes)? This bin-packing variant is likely NP-hard but the exact complexity class is open.

crossReferences.description: Both are impossibility results: cube dissection shows no finite decomposition into distinct smaller cubes exists, while Hilbert's 10th (MRDP theorem) shows no algorithm solves all Diophantine equations. Both use indirect arguments — infinite descent here, undecidability there

Both are geometric impossibility results: angle trisection shows certain constructions are impossible with compass and straightedge (via Galois theory), while cube dissection shows certain decompositions are impossible (via infinite descent). Different proof techniques for the same genre of result
OQ-01 formalizes collision pairs and minimum collision lower bounds — extending the cube dissection impossibility with quantitative results about how many cubes must share sizes
OQ-02 explores further extensions and variations of the cube dissection impossibility

Both are structural impossibility results where the proof identifies a fundamental obstruction: Abel-Ruffini's obstruction is the non-solvability of $S_5$ (group theory), while cube dissection's obstruction is the infinite descent forced by the surrounding geometry (combinatorics). Both reduce impossibility to a structural property that cannot be circumvented

The Erdős-Szekeres theorem (every sequence of length $mn+1$ has a monotone subsequence of length $m+1$ or $n+1$) uses the same proof pattern as cube dissection: construct a long chain (here, decreasing cube sizes; there, monotone subsequences), then use pigeonhole to derive a contradiction with finiteness

Ramsey theory and cube dissection share the infinite descent / pigeonhole methodology: both prove that sufficiently large structures must contain ordered substructures. The cube dissection proof constructs a strictly decreasing chain bounded by $|\text{cubes}|$; Ramsey constructs monochromatic cliques bounded by partition regularity

Hilbert's 3rd problem (Dehn's theorem): not all polyhedra of equal volume are equidecomposable — the Dehn invariant provides the obstruction. Both Hilbert-3 and cube dissection concern the limits of geometric decomposition, though the specific questions differ (equidecomposability vs. dissection into distinct-sized subcubes)
